sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the purpose of the order of draw and why the collection sequence prevents additive cross-contamination.
- Identify common blood collection tube colors and the additive contained in each.
- Explain why the order of draw matters for accurate coagulation, chemistry, hematology, and glucose results.
- Apply safe blood-collection practices, including personal protective equipment, sharps disposal, labeling, and patient identification.
- Recognize the assistant's supervised, policy-following role and escalate uncertainties, errors, refusals, and recollections to licensed staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a recipe: you add ingredients in a certain order so they don't mix the wrong way. The order of draw is that recipe for filling blood tubes.

### Question 2

If you use a spoon for salty soup and then stir a sweet dessert without washing it, a little salt sneaks in. The order of draw stops leftover chemicals from 'sneaking' into the next tube.

### Question 3

When you want a clean sample to check for germs, you grab that one first before anything else can get in the way.

### Question 4

The light-blue tube goes second because its test is very picky about other chemicals, so it gets a clean early turn.

### Question 5

The germ-check bottle is like taking the very first, cleanest sample so dirt from your fingers doesn't get mixed in and confuse the test.

### Question 6

Each tube color has its own special chemical inside, like different colored jars holding different ingredients. Light blue holds sodium citrate.

### Question 7

After the picky light-blue tube comes the plain serum tubes, which don't have an anticoagulant to cause trouble.

### Question 8

The purple tube waits its turn near the back of the line, just before the gray one.

### Question 9

The gray tube is the last in line, like the dessert saved for the end of a meal.

### Question 10

Using the same recipe every time means every batch turns out the same, so doctors can trust the results.

### Question 11

Carryover is like a tiny drop of one paint color getting onto the next color's brush and changing the shade.

### Question 12

Drawing the purple tube too early is like putting a strong ingredient into a recipe before its turn, which ruins the dish.

### Question 13

Calcium is like the glue that helps blood clump; citrate hides the glue away so the blood stays runny for testing.

### Question 14

The gel is like a wall that pops up between the liquid part and the clumpy part so they stay separated.

### Question 15

The gold tube has two helpers inside: one that helps the blood clot, and one that makes a wall to separate the liquid.

### Question 16

The plain red tube is like an empty jar with nothing added, so the blood does its natural thing and separates.

### Question 17

Without a 'keep-it-runny' chemical, the blood clumps and the clear liquid left behind is called serum.

### Question 18

The green tube's special ingredient is heparin, which keeps blood from clotting.

### Question 19

Heparin is the 'anti-clump' ingredient that keeps the blood smooth and liquid.

### Question 20

Plasma is the liquid part you get when the blood is kept from clumping, and the green tube does exactly that.

### Question 21

The purple tube holds EDTA, the ingredient that keeps blood cells fresh and unclumped for counting.

### Question 22

EDTA grabs onto calcium like a magnet and pulls it out of the way, so the blood can't clump.

### Question 23

When the doctor wants to count the red and white blood cells, the purple tube is the right container.

### Question 24

The gray tube holds two helpers: one keeps blood from clotting, and the other keeps sugar from being used up.

### Question 25

Fluoride is like a 'pause button' that stops the blood cells from eating the sugar before the lab measures it.

### Question 26

For a sugar check, the gray tube is the go-to because it keeps the sugar from changing.

### Question 27

Plasma is the liquid from blood that hasn't clumped; serum is the liquid left after the clump forms and is removed.

### Question 28

Plasma is the watery part of blood that stays liquid when a 'don't-clump' chemical is added.

### Question 29

When blood clumps, the leftover clear liquid on top is serum, like the juice around a curd.

### Question 30

The purple tube's chemical already has potassium in it, so measuring potassium in that tube is like weighing yourself while holding a heavy bag.

### Question 31

Citrate is like a sponge that soaks up calcium, so a calcium test in that tube would read too low.

### Question 32

Gently tipping the tube back and forth stirs the special chemical into the blood, like stirring sugar into tea.

### Question 33

The light-blue tube gets just a few gentle flips, enough to stir but not shake.

### Question 34

The purple tube gets a few more gentle flips than the blue one so its chemical spreads evenly.

### Question 35

If you don't stir the sugar into the tea, you get clumps at the bottom. If you don't mix the tube, you get blood clumps.

### Question 36

Imagine shaking a soda bottle too hard; the bubbles burst. Shaking blood too hard makes the red cells burst too.

### Question 37

Hemolysis is when the red blood cells pop like tiny water balloons and spill their color into the liquid.

### Question 38

Red blood cells are full of potassium; when they pop, all that potassium spills out and makes the number look higher than it really is.

### Question 39

The blue tube needs the right amount of blood for its amount of chemical; too little blood throws the measuring off.

### Question 40

Out of every 10 spoonfuls in the blue tube, 9 should be blood and only 1 is the chemical, so almost all of the tube is blood.

### Question 41

Each tube is like a measuring cup set to fill to exactly the right line by itself.

### Question 42

If the purple tube's anti-clump powder isn't stirred in, the blood clumps anyway.

### Question 43

Gloves are like a raincoat for your hands, keeping blood and germs off your skin.

### Question 44

A used needle goes straight into the special hard box, like putting a sharp knife away before it can poke anyone.

### Question 45

The safety device is like a cap that snaps over the sharp point all by itself so no one gets poked.

### Question 46

Never put the cap back on with your fingers; let the sharps box or the safety feature do the safe thing instead.

### Question 47

If you get poked, wash it right away and tell a grown-up in charge, fast, so you can get help.

### Question 48

Cleaning the skin first is like washing your hands before cooking so germs don't get into the food.

### Question 49

Write the name tag right away while you're still with the patient, so the tube never gets mixed up with someone else's.

### Question 50

Before taking anything, double-check who the person is using two clues, like their name and birthday.

### Question 51

The stretchy band is like a quick hug on the arm, only for a short moment, then let go.

### Question 52

Leave the band on too long and the blood gets 'thicker' and more crowded, making some counts look too high.

### Question 53

The assistant is the helpful teammate who gets everything ready and follows the rules while the trained professional does the poke.

### Question 54

When you're not sure about the steps, ask the person in charge instead of guessing.

### Question 55

If someone says no, we stop and tell the doctor, because their 'no' matters.

### Question 56

When a sample goes bad, the person in charge decides how to get a good one.

### Question 57

If someone is allergic to the cleaning wipe, we tell the doctor so they can pick a different one.

### Question 58

If the test needs an empty tummy and the person ate, we tell the doctor so they can decide what to do.

### Question 59

If you use the wrong container, own up to it right away so the team can fix it properly.

### Question 60

The blue tube is for the 'how fast does blood clump' test, so its special chemical keeps things just right.

### Question 61

The aPTT is another 'clumping-time' test, so it goes in the same blue tube as the PT.

### Question 62

For counting blood cells, the purple tube is the perfect home that keeps the cells from clumping.

### Question 63

For a sugar check, use the gray tube because it keeps the sugar from disappearing.

### Question 64

For the big 'body chemistry' check, the gold tube collects the clear serum the lab needs.

### Question 65

A blood culture bottle is like a garden where any germs hiding in the blood are grown so doctors can see what they are.

### Question 66

Fill the bottle that likes air first, then the one that hates air, so no extra air sneaks into the wrong bottle.

### Question 67

The butterfly tube has a little tunnel of air, so we fill a 'practice' tube first to get the air out before the real tubes.

### Question 68

For checking tiny amounts of metals like lead, you need a very 'clean' special blue tube.

### Question 69

The pink tube is the one used when the lab checks your blood type before a transfusion.

### Question 70

The gold tube takes its turn before the green tube, following the order like cars in a line.

### Question 71

If the sugar bowl got tipped into the salt shaker, the salt reading would look too high. Here, the tube's own potassium got mixed into the result.

### Question 72

If you mix up the steps, the test comes out wrong and the person has to be poked again — nobody wants that.

### Question 73

If a measuring cup is dirty, the recipe goes wrong; if the tube order is wrong, the doctor might make the wrong choice for the patient.

### Question 74

After the draw, write down when it happened and anything important, like taking notes in a diary.

### Question 75

Some ingredients spoil if left out, so we keep them cold or rush them to the lab, like putting milk in the fridge.

### Question 76

All the careful steps are there so the doctor gets a true answer and the patient gets the right care.

### Question 77

An anticoagulant is the 'don't-clump' ingredient that keeps blood runny inside the tube.

### Question 78

The tube is like a tiny vacuum cleaner that pulls in just the right amount of blood all by itself.

### Question 79

The colors are like the colored lids on spice jars that tell you what's inside without opening them.

### Question 80

The special chemical is already waiting inside the tube, ready to mix when the blood rushes in.

### Question 81

You can't use an 'anti-clump' chemical to measure how well blood clumps — it would mess up the answer.

### Question 82

Calcium is a key ingredient for clotting; EDTA hides it, so the clotting-time test gets the wrong answer.

### Question 83

To get serum, you need the blood to clump and leave clear liquid, so you use the tube that lets it clump.

### Question 84

Like old batteries that no longer work, old tubes might not fill right or their chemicals might be spent.

### Question 85

The assistant's job is to know the rules, set everything up right, and speak up if something seems off.
